newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Shipping Corp ploughs through low profits.
newsitem.headline: India's Shipping Corp ploughs through low profits.

text.p: Shipping Corporation of India, owner of more than 40 percent of the country's merchant fleet, may struggle with low profits for two years but there is fair weather ahead, a top SCI official said on Tuesday.
The continued recovery of the dry bulk cargo market from a 10-year low in September will be critical for SCI, company executive director K. Kothari told Reuters.
"The next one to two years may not be as good as we expect. It all depends on the dry bulk freight market," he said.
Kothari attributed the fall in 1996/97 net profit to 3.02 billion rupees ($84 million) from 3.23 billion the previous year, to the low freight rates and a tax payment of 450 million rupees.
Sickly dry bulk cargo rates and fierce competition from foreign lines have put Indian shipowners on the rack, analysts said. A saving grace for SCI are fairly firm tanker rates.
Analysts said they expected SCI, which is 80 percent owned by government, to improve its performance in 1997/98.
"While dry bulk freight is variable, tanker freight is long-term and constant," Kothari said.

There are 55 dry bulk and dry cargo vessels and 42 tankers among SCI's total fleet of 117 ships, reflecting the needs of an Indian economy whose growth is fuelled by burgeoning oil imports and exports made up mainly of food and raw materials.

The Baltic Freight Index for dry bulk cargo has recovered to 1,280 points in June from 992 in September -- its lowest level for a decade. But the recovery has been unconvincing, and today's levels are around 20 percent below December's.
Kothari said he would expect the medium-term, five-year outlook for the shipping industry to be very good.
He said SCI had drawn up a fleet expansion plan to add 44 ships at a total cost of 45 billion rupees ($1.2 billion) in the next five years to 2002.
"We will be able to generate funds for buying these ships internally and in both domestic and international capital markets," Kothari said.
On Monday, the surface transport ministry said SCI had been permitted to buy two crude oil tankers for $42 million each.
The two tankers, part of SCI's fleet expansion package, would be delivered by 1999, Kothari said.
Analysts reckon the government may have to divest more of its 80 percent stake in SCI if the company is to raise the money it needs for investment.
The 20 percent divested so far is held by state-owned Unit Trust of India, financial institutions, banks and the public.

Shyamali Roychowdhury of Lloyds Securities said the government could divest up to 75 percent of equity under current guidelines as shipping was a non-core sector industry, but did not foresee a long queque of buyers.
"There's a chance of further divestment," she said. "Right now SCI does not have the market charm as its free float is only 1.34 percent of its total equity," Roychowdhury said.
Analysts believe that SCI is less efficient than some private sector rivals.
"For instance, SCI's drydocking for maintenance of ships took nearly two to three months against 20 days for a private sector company ship," said one analyst.
"SCI also runs unremunerative passenger-cum-cargo ships on certain fixed routes which are obligatory and unprofitable," the analyst added.
But Roychowdhury saw merits in the balance of SCI's fleet, which also included containerships and offshore supply vessels.
"SCI is one of the most diversified companies in the world," he said. ($=35.8 rupees)
